Where is Bountiful, Utah, and how is the city laid out?

Bountiful is a city in Davis County, Utah, built on the slope between the Wasatch Range and the Great Salt Lake flats. Its elevation is about 4,771 feet, and the city covers roughly 13 square miles.

The original downtown sits at the base of the mountains. Homes climb the benches to the east, and the land to the west is flat and runs out toward the lake. Most of the ground east of the city is U.S. Forest Service land, so the hillside streets end where public land begins.

North Salt Lake lies to the south, Woods Cross and West Bountiful to the west, and Centerville to the north. Val Verda is the name used for the area in the southern part of the city. A seller on a bench street and a seller on the west side are dealing with very different lots, and buyers know it.

How did Bountiful start, and how fast has it grown?

Perrigrine Sessions and his family settled the site on September 27, 1847, which made it the second settlement in Utah after Salt Lake City. The place was first called Sessions Settlement and North Canyon Ward, and it was renamed Bountiful in 1855. The city incorporated in 1892, and electric lights came in 1907.

Growth was slow for a long time and then fast. The census counted 6,004 residents in 1950 and 17,039 in 1960. Bountiful was the largest city in Davis County until 1985, when Layton passed it.

The 2020 count came with 15,427 households and 15,945 housing units, and a median age of 35.1. Few lots are left to build on, so most sales here are resales of houses that already have decades of wear.

What does Bountiful's climate and terrain mean for a house?

Bountiful has a dry climate with about 23 inches of precipitation and about 59 inches of snow in a typical year. The record high is 104 degrees and the record low is minus 9, so roofs, furnaces and cooling systems all get used.

Heavy snow matters most on older roofs and on shaded driveways. Buyers and inspectors in a snow climate often look at the roof surface, the attic insulation and the gutters first. A seller who has not touched those in years should expect questions.

The Wasatch Fault runs along the base of the range, and the Utah Division of Emergency Management says more than 85 percent of Utahns live in the earthquake zone along the Wasatch Front. The same agency notes that unreinforced masonry buildings are a major concern along the fault. If your Bountiful house is older brick, a buyer may ask about chimneys, foundations and any past retrofit work.

  • Roof age and snow load on the east benches
  • Brick chimneys and masonry walls on older homes
  • Water drainage on steeper hillside lots
  • Furnace and water heater age

Which schools, roads and rail serve Bountiful?

Davis School District serves Bountiful. The nine elementary schools serving the city are Adelaide, Boulton, Bountiful, Holbrook, Meadowbrook, Muir, Oak Hills, Tolman and Valley View. The junior highs are Bountiful, Millcreek, Mueller Park and South Davis.

Interstate 15 is the main road, and the FrontRunner commuter rail has served Bountiful since April 2008. The Legacy Parkway opened on September 13, 2008, to take pressure off I-15. The narrow gap into Salt Lake County still causes slow traffic at rush hour, which is a talking point for buyers who commute south.

Other local anchors include Lakeview Hospital, the Bountiful Utah Temple (dedicated in 1995) and Mueller Park Canyon with its popular trail. Houses within a short drive of the canyon trailheads tend to get extra attention from buyers who hike.

Who provides power and water in Bountiful, and what do you do at move-out?

Bountiful City runs its own electric department, and it also handles utility billing. The power office is at 198 South 200 West, and the 24-hour outage line is 801-298-6072. Utility billing is at 801-298-6100.

The city's utility page says you must speak with a utility representative to start or end service, so a seller should call before the closing date rather than relying on an online form. City Hall is at 795 South Main Street. Final meter readings and the last bill are easier to sort out when the date of the sale is already fixed.

  • Call 801-298-6100 to schedule the end of your service
  • Ask for a final meter reading on the closing date
  • Confirm where the final bill should be mailed
  • Keep a copy of the closed account for your records

How are Bountiful property taxes billed and paid?

Bountiful property tax is billed by Davis County, and the bill is due November 30 each year. If that date lands on a weekend, it moves to the next business day. The county treasurer's office is at 61 South Main Street, Room 105, in Farmington, and the phone number is 801-451-3243.

Utah taxes a primary residence at a reduced share of value. Under Utah Code 59-2-103, residential property gets a 45 percent reduction, so only 55 percent of market value is taxed. The reduction covers no more than one acre of land per residential unit.

If a lender escrows your taxes, the lender may pay through a third-party service, and the county notes that can delay posting by several days. Check the account before you list.

How do you appeal a Bountiful home value in Davis County?

You file a Board of Equalization appeal with the Davis County Controller by the deadline printed on your Notice of Property Market Valuation. The county's online form takes one application per parcel, and it asks you to state your own opinion of the value as of January 1.

The county lists the kinds of evidence it accepts. A recent closing statement, a full appraisal, at least three comparable sales within one mile, an income statement, a documented factual error or a record of a damaged condition can each support a case. Only the current year's market value can be appealed, not the tax rate. The controller's phone number is 801-451-3323.

If you sell mid-year, the appeal and the tax bill still follow the property. Tell the buyer's side what is pending so the title company can handle any refund correctly.

What do Bountiful sellers usually run into?

Sellers in Bountiful most often deal with an older house, a hillside lot, or a buyer who needs a quick, simple closing. A cash sale removes the lender appraisal and the repair negotiation that often follow a listing, and it lets you pick the closing date.

  • Older homes that need roof, electrical or plumbing work before a retail buyer will lend
  • Inherited houses where several family members have to agree before anyone signs
  • Rentals with tenants in place and a lease that runs past the sale date
  • Overdue repairs that make a traditional listing hard to price

Bountiful's resale pool is large because the city is close to Salt Lake City and has the FrontRunner line. That helps a well-kept house on the market. It does less for a property that needs work, which is where an as-is sale tends to fit.

Bountiful is in Davis County, and the Davis County treasurer bills and collects the property tax. The office is at 61 South Main Street in Farmington, and the phone number is 801-451-3243.

When is Bountiful property tax due?

Property tax in Bountiful is due November 30. If that date falls on a weekend, Davis County moves the deadline to the next business day. A late payment carries a penalty of the greater of $10 or 2.5 percent per parcel.

Is there a way to lower the taxable value on a Bountiful house?

A primary residence already gets the 45 percent residential reduction under Utah Code 59-2-103. If you think the market value on your valuation notice is too high, you can file a Board of Equalization appeal with the Davis County Controller by the date printed on the notice.

Who do I call to stop electric service when I sell?

Call Bountiful City utility billing at 801-298-6100. The city says you must speak with a representative to start or end service, so schedule it before closing.

Can I sell a Bountiful house that has tenants or needs repairs?

Yes. Houses with tenants, deferred repairs or an inherited title can be sold as they are. Tell the buyer about the lease terms and the condition up front so the closing date and any move-out terms are clear.

Where is Cedar City, Utah, and what is it like to live there?

Cedar City is the largest city in Iron County, in southwestern Utah, about 250 miles south of Salt Lake City and 170 miles north of Las Vegas on Interstate 15. It sits in Cedar Valley on the western edge of the Markagunt Plateau, at an elevation above 5,600 feet.

St. George is about 50 miles to the southwest, and Interstate 70 is about 75 miles north. Zion National Park, Bryce Canyon National Park and Cedar Breaks National Monument are all within a day trip. The name comes from the juniper trees early settlers called cedars.

Most buyers here either work in town, attend the university, or are drawn by the access to the parks and the high country. A seller who knows which group their house suits can talk about it more plainly.

How did Cedar City begin, and how big is it now?

Cedar City was founded on November 11, 1851, when Mormon pioneers from Parowan came to build an iron works. The town moved to a new site closer to the works in 1855, out of the Coal Creek flood plain. It incorporated on February 18, 1868, and a railroad connection in 1923 made it a gateway for park visitors. Mining continued until the 1980s.

The 2020 count was up 22.1 percent from 2010, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 41,871. That is fast growth for a city of this size. The 2020 census listed 11,824 households and 12,723 housing units, with a median age of 26.2.

A young median age reflects the university. It also means plenty of rentals, which matters if you are a landlord thinking about selling.

What does the economy depend on in Cedar City?

Cedar City's economy rests on Southern Utah University, a small manufacturing base, tourism and home construction. SUU is the largest employer in Iron County, and the Iron County School District is next in the 2019 employer list.

  • Southern Utah University: 2,000 to 2,999 employees
  • Iron County School District: 1,000 to 1,999
  • Intermountain Health: 500 to 1,500
  • Cedar City Corporation, Genpak, federal government, State of Utah and Walmart: 250 to 499 each

SUU reported a fall 2025 headcount of 15,825 students, up 2.47 percent from the year before, including more than 3,691 fully online students. A Gardner Policy Institute study of fiscal year 2023 counted 2,687 direct SUU jobs and more than 5,000 jobs once indirect effects were included. The same study put out-of-region visitor spending at about $7 million, tied to events such as the Utah Shakespeare Festival and athletics.

Because a lot of the local economy follows the school calendar and the festival season, demand for houses and rentals can shift with the term and the summer. That is worth knowing before you set a closing date.

What does Cedar City's weather mean for a house?

Cedar City has a semi-arid climate with cold winters, hot summers and about 11 inches of precipitation a year. In the 1991 to 2020 normals, the January daily high averages 42.8 degrees and the low 18.0, while July highs average 91.0.

Snow is a real factor. The city averages about 47.8 inches a year, and January 1949 holds the single-month record of 36.9 inches. The record low is minus 26 and the record high is 105.

That range is hard on exteriors. Freeze and thaw cycles crack driveways and stucco, dry summers fade roofing, and cold nights stress older plumbing and water heaters. Buyers who tour in winter will notice insulation, windows and heating costs quickly.

  • Roof condition after heavy snow seasons
  • Exposed pipes and hose bibs in cold snaps
  • Cracks in concrete and stucco from freeze and thaw
  • Heating system age and efficiency

Which schools, roads and services does Cedar City have?

The Iron County School District serves Cedar City, with two high schools, Cedar High School and Canyon View High School. Southern Utah University is the main college, and the city is also known for the Utah Shakespeare Festival and the Utah Summer Games.

Interstate 15 is the main route. A Union Pacific branch line runs along the western edge of town, and the Cedar City Regional Airport has Delta Connection flights. The city also has a local bus system. Cedar City Utah Temple was dedicated on December 10, 2017.

City Hall is at 10 North Main Street, open 8 am to 5 pm. The City Council meets on Wednesdays at 5:30 pm and streams on YouTube, except on the fifth Wednesday of a month. The city runs a water usage app called MY360 that lets residents view their water use, which is handy when closing out an account.

How does Iron County assess and bill property tax in Cedar City?

Iron County assesses and bills Cedar City homes, and its offices are at 68 South 100 East in Parowan. The Assessor is at 435-477-8310. The county says property is valued by its condition and ownership as of January 1, using cost, income and market approaches.

Appeals go through the Iron County Auditor at 435-477-8333. The Board is usually in session from late September through early October, and the assessed value is presumed correct, so you need firm evidence of a lower market value. A primary residence is taxed at 55 percent of value, and Utah Code 59-2-103 caps the reduction at one acre of land per residential unit.

Unpaid current-year taxes become delinquent on December 1, and Utah's property tax calendar describes a tax sale for parcels that stay unpaid for years. A seller with back taxes should talk to the treasurer before listing.

What else is in Iron County besides Cedar City?

Iron County covers about 3,300 square miles along Utah's western border with Nevada, and Parowan is the county seat. The 2020 census counted 57,289 people in the county, so Cedar City holds most of them. Enoch and Parowan are the other named towns nearby.

The county runs from desert basins in the west to high plateau meadows and forest in the east. Brian Head, at 11,307 feet, is the highest point and Cedar Breaks National Monument sits on the Markagunt Plateau. A seller on the east side of town and a seller near the desert edge can face very different weather, so say which one you are when you describe the house.

What do Cedar City sellers usually face?

Cedar City sellers often have a rental that has aged, a house that needs updating, or a property they inherited from a family member who lived out of state. Selling for cash can fit those cases because there is no lender appraisal and no list of buyer repair requests.

  • Student and seasonal rentals with turnover damage
  • Houses with older roofs, windows and heating systems
  • Inherited property where heirs live in other states
  • Vacant houses that sit empty through a cold winter

If the house is vacant, winter matters. A cold, empty house can freeze pipes, and a summer-vacant one can pick up dust and weeds quickly. Many sellers in a spot like this want one clear closing date instead of months of showings.

What county is Cedar City in, and who sets my property value?

Cedar City is in Iron County, and the Iron County Assessor sets the value. The assessor's office is in Parowan at 68 South 100 East, and the phone number is 435-477-8310.

When can I appeal my Cedar City property value?

Iron County real property appeals are due September 15 by 5:00 PM, or 45 days after the valuation notice is mailed if that is later. File with the Iron County Auditor at 435-477-8333.

What is the property tax due date in Cedar City?

Property tax is due November 30, and unpaid taxes become delinquent on December 1. Iron County mails the tax notices around November 1.

How big is Cedar City?

Cedar City had 35,235 residents at the 2020 census, and the Census Bureau estimated 41,871 for July 1, 2025. It is the largest city in Iron County.

Can I sell a rental house in Cedar City with tenants in it?

Yes, a house can be sold with tenants in place or after they leave. Share the lease dates and rent details early so the closing date and move-out terms are agreed in writing.

Where is Clearfield, Utah, and what does the map look like?

Clearfield is a compact city in north-central Davis County, about 30 miles north of Salt Lake City, with Hill Air Force Base along its northeastern edge. It covers roughly 7.75 square miles, which makes it one of the smaller cities on the north Wasatch Front.

Sunset is to the north, Clinton to the northwest, Syracuse and West Point to the west, and Layton wraps the south and east. Streets follow a grid, with the main roads running close to north-south and east-west. The land is flat. The lowest spot is about 4,314 feet at 1000 West and Antelope Drive, and the highest is 4,711 feet in the northeast corner, on base property.

The Weber and Davis Canal runs along the east and northeast edge. Interstate 15 follows the eastern side of town, and the Wasatch Range rises beyond it, with Ben Lomond Peak at 9,712 feet.

How did Clearfield get its start?

Richard and Emily Hamblin settled the area in 1877 and called it Sand Ridge. The Utah Central Railroad crossed the area in 1869, and a canal that arrived in 1884 sparked a population jump. Clearfield became a town on July 17, 1922, and a city on March 21, 1946.

War changed the place. Hill Field began construction in 1940, and the Navy commissioned the Clearfield Naval Supply Depot on April 10, 1943, to supply the Pacific Fleet. The Navy phased the depot out in 1962, and private firms moved in. That site is now the Freeport Center.

The jump from 982 people in 1940 to 4,723 in 1950 explains the housing stock. Much of the city's growth came in the postwar decades, so a good share of its houses are likely several decades old.

Who employs people in Clearfield?

Hill Air Force Base, the Freeport Center and a handful of manufacturers carry the local economy. The base is Davis County's largest employer, with nearly 23,000 military and civilian personnel, and it accounts for about 12 percent of the county's economy. As of 2018 it was the sixth-largest employer in Utah.

The Freeport Center covers 680 acres, with 78 buildings and more than 7 million square feet. About 70 companies and roughly 7,000 workers operate there, and most buildings have both a truck dock and a Union Pacific rail dock. The name comes from Utah's 1966 Freeport Law, which exempted inventory held for sale from property tax.

Two newer business areas, Legend Hills off I-15 and the planned Falcon Hill aerospace area on the base's west and southwest side, point to more aerospace work nearby. Base assignments can change, and military families often need a fast sale when orders arrive.

Clearfield has four seasons, about 20.75 inches of precipitation and about 24 inches of snow a year. The average annual temperature is 53 degrees, with a July 2002 record high of 108 and a January 1937 record low of minus 26.

Winter inversions can trap heavy air pollution along this part of the Wasatch Front. That can matter to buyers who care about indoor air, filters and furnace condition. The Wasatch Fault runs along the western base of the mountains, and the Utah Division of Emergency Management warns that older unreinforced masonry buildings are at greater risk in a strong quake.

  • Brick chimneys and masonry porches
  • Roof age after years of snow load

Clearfield sits in the Davis School District. Its public schools include Clearfield High School, North Davis Junior High and elementary schools such as South Clearfield, Hill Field and Holt.

Interstate 15 runs along the eastern edge, and a FrontRunner commuter rail stop opened in 2008. That gives commuters a rail option along the Wasatch Front. Davis County also lists Clearfield as one of the FrontRunner station cities, alongside Woods Cross, Farmington and Layton.

Because the city is small and flat, many houses are a short drive from the base gates, the Freeport Center and the freeway. That convenience is one of the first things buyers ask about.

How close is Hill Air Force Base, and why does it matter to sellers?

Hill Air Force Base borders Clearfield, Layton, Riverdale, Roy and Sunset, and its longest border is shared with Clearfield and Layton. Hill Field opened on November 7, 1940, and became Hill Air Force Base on February 5, 1948. Wartime employment peaked at just over 22,000 people in 1943.

The 75th Air Base Wing hosts the Ogden Air Logistics Complex, the 388th and 419th Fighter Wings and more than 50 other units. The Hill Aerospace Museum on base opened in 1981. For a Clearfield seller, the base means a steady pool of local buyers and renters, along with the occasional sudden move when someone gets orders and has little time to prepare a house.

How does Davis County bill Clearfield property tax?

Davis County bills Clearfield property taxes, and the payment is due November 30. If that date falls on a weekend, the county treasurer moves the due date to the next business day, which is December 1 or December 2 depending on the day.

Card payments carry a fee paid to the card company, and electronic check payments do not. After November 30, the penalty is the greater of $10 or 2.5 percent per parcel. If you pay in full by January 31, it drops to the greater of $10 or 1 percent. Interest follows after that at a rate between 7.25 and 10 percent.

Utah Code 59-2-103 gives residential property a 45 percent reduction in value, so a primary residence is taxed on 55 percent. Rental houses do not qualify unless the tenant lives there as a primary residence, so Clearfield landlords usually see a higher bill.

What do Clearfield sellers usually deal with?

Clearfield sellers often own a mid-century house with deferred updates, a rental that has run its course, or a home they must sell quickly because of a job or military move. A cash sale can close on a date you choose and skips the usual repair requests that come with a lender's appraisal.

  • Inherited property with several heirs and no clear plan

When you sell, expect the title company to split the property tax bill between you and the buyer based on the closing date. Ask for that proration in writing, and confirm whether your lender has been paying the tax from an escrow account, since the county warns that third-party services can be slow to post payments.

Clearfield property tax is due November 30. If November 30 falls on a weekend, the due date moves to the next business day, and penalties start after that day.

The Freeport Center is a 680-acre manufacturing and distribution complex on the former Clearfield Naval Supply Depot. It has 78 buildings, about 70 companies and roughly 7,000 workers.

Does Hill Air Force Base affect Clearfield housing?

Yes, the base is next door and is Davis County's largest employer, with nearly 23,000 personnel. Many Clearfield homes are bought and sold by people tied to the base.

Can I sell a Clearfield house that needs repairs?

Yes. Houses can be sold as they are, with repairs left undone. Tell the buyer about the roof, heating, plumbing and electrical so the terms are clear before closing.

Where is Cottonwood Heights, Utah?

Cottonwood Heights is a city on the east bench of the Salt Lake Valley in Salt Lake County, south of Holladay and Murray, east of Midvale and north of Sandy. Its official nickname is the City between the canyons.

A high ridge separates the Big Cottonwood and Little Cottonwood creek valleys, and at the eastern edge both valleys narrow into canyons in the Wasatch Mountains. The elevation is about 4,820 feet, and the city covers 9.23 square miles. Interstate 215 runs along the northern border, and State Routes 190 and 210 reach the canyon mouths near the eastern edge.

Salt Lake County itself held 1,185,238 people in 2020. Big Cottonwood Canyon leads to the Solitude and Brighton ski resorts, and Little Cottonwood Canyon leads to Snowbird and Alta, so the city sits at the doorway to winter recreation.

Only State Routes 190 and 210 enter the city proper, and State Route 152 touches it at a single point. For a seller, that means traffic on the canyon roads in ski season is part of the daily picture, and a street close to the canyon mouths feels different from one near I-215.

Cottonwood Heights was an unincorporated area until voters approved a referendum in May 2004, and the city incorporated on January 14, 2005. On January 8, 2008, the city council voted to start its own police department and leave the Salt Lake County Sheriff's contract.

The area's roots go back further. An old paper mill, the Cottonwood Paper Mill, was built in 1883 by the Deseret News. The city is also building a multi-use trail along Big Cottonwood Creek within its borders.
